source.title: Jailbreak Antidote: Runtime Safety-Utility Balance via Sparse Representation Adjustment in Large Language Models
source.authors: Guo-Bin Shen; Dong-Cheng Zhao; Yi-Ting Dong; Xiang He; Yi Zeng

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether jailbreak attacks, including GCG adversarial suffixes, succeed against aligned chat models, using Defense Success Rate rather than the original sources’ fine-tuning or per-token KL methods.
record.gate_note: The paper reports DSR under attacks and a runtime activation defense. It does not test fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples, per-token KL, compliant prefill, or decoding changes. The reported comparisons of defense methods are not included as separate rows except where needed to record baseline versus Antidote results. Descriptions of prior work are not treated as results.
record.test_reason: The paper is mainly a runtime activation-steering defense, but Table A.4 reports no-defense DSR under GCG adversarial suffixes for three chat models. That measures how often a suffix attack defeats refusal, which bears on V4's suffix part. All other rows either average over non-suffix attacks (persona, tense, PAIR, AutoDAN) or report the study's own defense, so they do not bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that shifting about 5% of last-token hidden dimensions along a PCA safety direction at runtime raises DSR across nine models and ten attacks while preserving AlpacaEval utility. They also note that negative α turns the method into an attack, a potential vulnerability.
record.recipe_differences: This is runtime hidden-state activation adjustment, not fine-tuning on a small dataset or per-token KL measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: DSR varies across models and attack methods; the paper also reports trade-offs as scaling factor α and sparsity k change.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding a direction to about 5% of last-token hidden-state dimensions raises DSR roughly as much as adjusting all dimensions, with less utility loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-relevant activation directions are sparse in hidden dimensions and steerable at inference.

fits_no_version.finding: Negative steering (α<0) along the safety direction lowers safety below baseline. This is an induced white-box attack.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation steering against the refusal direction weakens refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: The last prompt token's hidden state best separates benign from harmful prompts (Figures A.3–A.6). This concerns prompt positions, not response positions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmfulness is most linearly readable at the final prompt token.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the cataloged DSR values. The adaptive-attack table covers three models; several sparsity comparisons are described qualitatively and shown in figures without exact values.

untested.parts: No per-token KL over response positions. The token-position analysis is over prompt tokens.
Compliant prefilling and decoding changes are not tested. Only GCG suffix baselines are relevant.
No weight or rank localization. Sparsity concerns activation dimensions of a steering direction.
No analysis of the data or objective causing shallowness.
No token-depth deepening training. The DSA checkpoint appears only as a baseline under mixed non-prefill attacks.

missing.what: Per-attack no-defense DSR for GCG and random-search suffix attacks across all nine models (static attacks).

record.verdict_notes: The paper is primarily a defense paper (close to T4). It counts as a test only through the undefended GCG baselines. Most extracted rows record the study's own method against baseline and are relinked to none. Table 1 duplicates the Gemma-2-2B-it values for Qwen-1.5-7B-it. No uncertainty estimates are given. Suffix attack success in the main tables uses static artifacts from JailbreakBench.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
The study evaluates GCG suffixes and other jailbreak attacks, but not compliant prefilling or decoding changes.
The paper manipulates sparse hidden-state dimensions, not weights or ranks.
It does not test whether data or training objectives produce first-token shallowness.
It does not train safety to be deeper across response tokens or evaluate whether such training holds up.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7B-chat
rows.operation_detail: Apply adaptive GCG attack; compare baseline with Jailbreak Antidote.
rows.note: GCG is described as appending an adversarial suffix; DSR is the percentage of harmful prompts blocked.
rows.check: The relevant number is the no-defense DSR of 46%, meaning GCG succeeds on about 54% of prompts. The Antidote value (83) is the study's own method and should not be the row's value. The judge requires a rating of 10 to count a jailbreak, which is strict.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-it
rows.operation_detail: Adjust top-ranked dimensions of the last-token hidden state using the masked safety direction.
rows.measure: DSR and Win Rate safety-utility balance
rows.value: 5% of dimensions adjusted gives performance described as nearly identical to 100%
rows.note: The authors explicitly state that 5% adjustment yields performance nearly identical to adjusting 100%; this concerns activation dimensions, not weights or ranks.
rows.check: This is a sparsity ablation of the study's own method on activation dimensions, not weights or ranks. It is not V5.

rows.subject: Qwen-2-7B-it

rows.value: At k = 100%, Win Rate drops sharply; at k = 5%, utility impact is described as minimal
rows.note: Qualitative description in the text; no numeric figure values are stated.
rows.check: This is a sparsity ablation of the study's own method; it measures utility, not safety localization in parameters.

relationships.condition: Undefended Llama-2-7B/13B-chat and Llama-3-8B-it under adaptive GCG suffixes, with a strict judge (rating 10 required)
relationships.reason: GCG suffixes defeat refusal on only about 27–54% of harmful prompts (no-defense DSR 46/70/73), not wholesale (r12, r15, r18).
relationships.display_finding: Undefended defense success rates were 46, 70 and 73, so GCG suffixes defeated refusal on only about 27–54% of harmful prompts.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
